analysis.one_liner: Lets bankrupt U.S. territories wipe out unsecured public debts while compensating small, local creditors.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 19 cosponsors and referred to three committees, the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let Puerto Rico (and any U.S. territory meeting two of three hardship tests: shrinking population, a major disaster, or per-person debt above $15,000) legally cancel its unsecured public debt — bonds, loans, and derivatives — rather than repay it for decades. It would also create a $15 billion federal fund to compensate certain creditors, deliberately favoring Puerto Rico residents, small local banks and credit unions, pension plans, and ordinary people who held the island's bonds, while excluding hedge funds, big banks with over $2 billion in assets, and bond insurers. A third part would set up an independent commission to audit all Puerto Rico public debt issued since 1972 and publish the findings.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of Puerto Rico, whose government could redirect money now going to bond payments toward schools, health care, and services. Also protected: Puerto Rico pension plans, local banks and credit unions, worker associations, small businesses, and individual island residents who held Puerto Rico bonds — they would be first in line for compensation from the $15 billion fund. Off-island small investors and open-end mutual funds would get compensation only if their managers waived fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Puerto Rico residents and small local creditors

how_it_helps.text: A territory can discharge unsecured debt if it meets two of three criteria: population down more than 5% in ten years, a major federal disaster in the past five years, or per capita debt above $15,000. Puerto Rico, hit by Hurricanes Irma and Maria in September 2017, meets all three.
The discharge requires a vote of the territory's legislature and its governor, and can be used only once every seven years, so it is a deliberate, elected choice rather than a unilateral default.

Secured debt (debt backed by specific pledged collateral) survives; only unsecured obligations are wiped out, and pension and retiree health obligations are expressly excluded from discharge and must still be repaid in full.

The $15 billion compensation fund is split evenly between creditors domiciled in Puerto Rico and others, and it excludes financial institutions with more than $2 billion in assets, hedge funds and unregistered investment funds, bond insurers, and parties to swaps and repurchase agreements — so Wall Street-style creditors lose their claims with no payout, while ordinary holders are made whole first.

An independent commission would audit every debt issued since fiscal 1972, with power to compel testimony and documents, and publish a public database of how Puerto Rico incurred and used borrowed money.

analysis.who_pays: Unsecured bondholders — hedge funds, mutual funds, bond insurers, and large financial institutions — lose their claims outright, with compensation only for the smaller holders the fund covers. Federal taxpayers bear a $15 billion emergency appropriation to fund the compensation, designated as an emergency so it bypasses normal budget limits.

drawbacks.text: Wiping out creditors' legal claims through a legislative vote, outside a court-managed bankruptcy, invites constitutional challenges — creditors could argue the discharge takes their property without just compensation under the Fifth Amendment. The bill tries to head this off by routing all such disputes into Puerto Rico courts within 180 days and barring creditors from raising the takings claim elsewhere, a provision that would itself likely be tested.

The $15 billion fund is an emergency-designated federal appropriation with no offsetting spending cuts, adding to the deficit; and if eligible claims exceed the fund, every claimant in each pool is cut pro rata, so even protected small creditors may be paid less than they are owed.

Using a disaster as a qualifying criterion discharges debt that predated the storm by decades; creditors who lent in good faith years before the hurricanes absorb the loss, which could raise borrowing costs for all territories afterward.
The relief is partial: pension and retiree health obligations are carved out and must be repaid in full, so the bill does not touch the largest single category of Puerto Rico's unfunded burdens.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people in Puerto Rico the upside is large — decades of debt payments freed up for public services at the cost of losses borne mostly by professional bond investors, with a federally funded cushion for the small local creditors who would otherwise be ruined. The serious costs are real but indirect: a $15 billion unoffset federal appropriation, unsettled constitutional ground, and the precedent that debts owed to outside lenders can be discharged by legislative vote. On balance, the design deliberately directs the pain away from island residents and toward concentrated financial creditors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2018 and sent to three committees, one of which sent it to a subcommittee, and then the 115th Congress ended in January 2019 without any committee action, hearing, or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velázquez introduced the bill on September 13, 2018, joined by 19 Democratic cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to three House committees — Natural Resources, Judiciary, and Budget — splitting jurisdiction across panels.
Eleven days later it went to the Natural Resources subcommittee on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs; the record shows no hearing, markup, or vote in any committee.

The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 with the bill still stalled in committee, so every provision — the debt discharge, the $15 billion compensation fund, and the debt audit commission — expired without any action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unsecured Puerto Rico creditors — hedge funds, mutual funds, bond insurers, and large banks holding the island's debt — are better off, because their claims survived intact under the existing PROMESA restructuring instead of being discharged. Puerto Rico residents and its government gain nothing; the island continued paying under court-supervised debt restructuring instead of getting legislative relief.

for.name: Rep. Nydia Velázquez

for.name: 19 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 19 were Democrats, including Reps. Grijalva (Natural Resources ranking member), Waters, Jayapal, Khanna, McGovern, DeLauro, Schakowsky, and Serrano.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill was sent to a subcommittee on September 24, 2018 and stayed there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor for a vote; with no committee action reported, there was nothing to schedule.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; with Republicans controlling the House, the bill drew no Republican support and died in committee without a vote.

industries.industry: Hedge funds and mutual funds holding Puerto Rico bonds
industries.note: Their unsecured Puerto Rico claims would be discharged outright, and hedge funds and unregistered funds are excluded from the compensation fund entirely. Their interest in full repayment runs against island residents who would bear the taxes and service cuts to pay them.

Insurers that sold protection on Puerto Rico bonds would lose payouts and are expressly barred from compensation. They profit from guaranteeing government debt, a cost ultimately paid by the issuing government's residents.

industries.industry: Large banks and financial institutions (over $2 billion in assets)
industries.note: They are excluded from compensation, and swaps and repurchase-agreement parties lose their claims too. Local Puerto Rico banks and credit unions, by contrast, would be compensated — the fund sorts creditors by size and locality.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico local banks, credit unions, pension plans, and resident bondholders
industries.note: They would be first in line for the $15 billion compensation fund, with their claims paid ahead of outside professional investors. Their interest and island residents' interest line up.

industries.industry: Puerto Rico government and its agencies
industries.note: A discharge once every seven years would free the Commonwealth from decades of unsecured debt service, redirecting money to services; a commissioned audit would also expose how the debt was run up.

The audit commission would scrutinize every bond deal since 1972 and publish the role of each banker who executed it, and a standing territorial right to discharge debt would weaken the market's assumption that government bonds are always repaid in full.
